## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] In the Movement Disorders systematic review of neuroimaging-based AI studies, the authors report that the majority of studies aimed to distinguish PD patients from healthy controls (54%) or atypical parkinsonian syndromes (25%), whereas prognostic or interventional studies were sparse. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11657025/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] Reviews report inconsistent validation practice in PD machine learning: in one sample of 113 studies only 65.5% (74/113) used a holdout test set to avoid potentially inflated accuracies and 38.9% (44/113) did not report on how or if models were tuned, and a review of machine learning within PPMI finds significant variability in the types of data, models, and validation procedures used across studies. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11112052/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9968811/
- [statement] Neuroimaging-focused reviews flag quality and translation concerns: the Movement Disorders review reports that only 20% of evaluated studies passed all five MQC and calls the number of studies failing to pass the MQC alarming, a brain-imaging machine learning review states that several issues must be addressed before these solutions can be safely integrated into clinical practice, and a deep learning review identifies a lack of data availability and interpretability of models. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11657025/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10394631/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37200116/
- [statement] External validation is uncommon in the reviewed literature: the neuroimaging review reports that very few studies employed external test sets (8%), where accuracy was significantly lower, and the later biomarker review reports that only 20 (7.6%) of the studies met its external-validation definition and that in ten within-study comparisons external performance fell in eight. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11657025/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13702696/
- [statement] Deep learning is not uniformly superior: a review of deep learning in PD reports state-of-the-art performance in many PD-related tasks by outperforming conventional machine learning approaches, while a gait meta-analysis reports that ML models achieved the best results for classifying healthy patients (H&Y0: 95.7% to 98.2%) and DL approaches performed better for classifying higher severity levels (>92%). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37200116/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13362068/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] One review cites a UK autopsy study that found the misdiagnosis rate of PD is 24%, and a neuroimaging review states that the heterogeneous disease phenotype and overlapping symptoms with atypical parkinsonian syndromes (APS) contribute to high misdiagnosis rates. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11112052/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11657025/
- [statement] High reported accuracy coexists with weak evidence quality: a gait meta-analysis states that its GRADE analysis revealed low-quality evidence for precision and F1 score and very-low quality for accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity, and the biomarker review reports median best-model accuracy of 95.3% while 259 studies (98.1%) were at high overall risk of bias under its adapted PROBAST rules. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13362068/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13702696/
- [statement] In a machine learning study of longitudinal clinical data from a Parkinson's progression cohort, the authors report projections of disease progression 5 years after initial diagnosis with an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.92 for the slower progressing group and 0.95 ± 0.02 for the fast-progressing group. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9758217/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] The authors of the progression study report that they replicated their findings in an independent cohort, released the analytical code, and identified serum neurofilament light as a significant indicator of fast disease progression among other key biomarkers of interest. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9758217/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Data leakage inflates reported accuracy in PD machine learning: the neuroimaging review reports that data leakage was associated with a significant inflation of accuracies, and a separate study reports that without overt features all models exhibited superficially acceptable F1 scores but failed catastrophically in specificity, with the authors attributing high accuracy when overt features were included to data leakage rather than genuine predictive power. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11657025/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12383348/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Systematic reviews of machine learning in PD report a translation gap: one states that very few ML systems have been adopted for real-world use despite the large number of studies published every year, and a later review concludes that reported performance has advanced faster than evidence of generalizability and clinical implementation. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11112052/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13702696/
- [statement] A preprint auditing evaluation protocols reports that subject-aware splitting reduced voice AUROC from 0.892 to 0.780, and that supervised probe selection before splitting inflated transcriptomic AUROC from 0.711 to 0.998. (low confidence) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14533 · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] The biomarker review states that its proportions describe the sample assessed, not the entire PD machine learning literature, and an earlier review likewise describes its work as sampling current ML practices in PD applications. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13702696/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11112052/

## Research summary — AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression

Systematic reviews of machine learning in Parkinson's disease report a translation gap: very few systems have been adopted for real-world use, external validation is uncommon and accuracy is lower on external test sets, and data leakage is associated with inflated accuracy. The reviews also report high headline accuracy alongside low-quality evidence and a high risk of bias in most assessed studies, and a preprint reports that subject-aware splitting lowers reported performance. A machine learning study of longitudinal clinical data reports projections of progression and a replication in an independent cohort. The reviews' proportions describe the samples assessed, not the whole literature.
